explain.say: Most bricks start as clay or shale dug from a quarry. It is crushed and mixed with water until it is soft and easy to shape, a bit like modelling clay.

explain.say: In a modern works, the clay is pushed through a die as a long rectangular column, like toothpaste, and a row of wires slices it into bricks. Others are pressed into moulds, which makes the dent called a frog.

explain.say: Then they are fired in a kiln at around 1,000 degrees Celsius. The clay changes chemically and its grains fuse together, making a hard, weatherproof brick that can never soften back into clay.

faq.a: Most are extruded: stiff clay is forced through a rectangular die and wire-cut, often with holes through them to save clay and help firing. Others are pressed or thrown into moulds, sometimes by hand for a rustic look.
asks: Why do some bricks have holes in them?

faq.q: Why are bricks dried before firing?
faq.a: Fresh bricks contain lots of water. Drying them slowly first lets the water escape gently; otherwise it would boil into steam in the kiln and crack them.
asks: What happens if you fire wet clay?

faq.q: What happens to clay in a brick kiln?
faq.a: Heat drives out water locked inside the clay minerals, then at the highest temperatures parts of the clay melt slightly and glue the grains together. This change is permanent, turning clay into ceramic.
Most clays contain iron. When fired with plenty of air, the iron forms red iron oxide, like rust. Clays with little iron fire to cream or yellow, and less air in the kiln can make darker bricks.

faq.q: How long have people made bricks?
faq.a: Sun-dried mud bricks were used at Jericho and other early towns over 9,000 years ago. Fired bricks, much stronger and waterproof, came later and were used widely by the Indus, Mesopotamian and Roman builders.

facts: Most clay bricks are fired at around 900 to 1,200 °C.
The red colour of most bricks comes from iron oxide formed from iron in the clay.
